subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean descent develops jaundice and dark urine 3 days after beginning primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. His hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, reticulocyte count is 9%, indirect bilirubin is 4.3 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase is markedly elevated. Serum haptoglobin is undetectable, and the peripheral smear shows bite cells.
question: Which of the following best explains the low serum haptoglobin in this patient?

options.text: Decreased hepatic synthesis of haptoglobin due to hepatocellular injury
Urinary loss of haptoglobin caused by glomerular damage
Consumption of haptoglobin by bilirubin in the circulation
Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis, and the complex is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system
Haptoglobin is a positive acute phase reactant whose level falls during inflammation

explanation_correct: Haptoglobin is a plasma glycoprotein that binds free hemoglobin liberated by intravascular hemolysis, forming a complex that is removed by the reticuloendothelial system. This conserves iron and prevents hemoglobin-induced renal injury, but it also consumes haptoglobin, so the serum level falls rapidly and is a sensitive marker of intravascular hemolysis. This patient has G6PD deficiency triggered by primaquine, with bite cells, low haptoglobin, high LDH, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Haptoglobin is synthesized in the liver, but this patient has no evidence of hepatocellular injury; low haptoglobin here reflects consumption by free hemoglobin.
explanation_incorrect.B: Haptoglobin is retained in plasma by its high molecular weight and is not lost in urine unless there is severe glomerular disease, which is absent in this case.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bilirubin does not bind or consume haptoglobin; the relevant ligand is free hemoglobin released from lysed red blood cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: Haptoglobin is an acute phase reactant whose level rises with inflammation, not falls; the low value here reflects hemolysis.

educationalObjective: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin during intravascular hemolysis and is consumed in the process, so a low serum haptoglobin is a sensitive marker of hemolysis.
